questions.q: 'Alternative Dispute Resolution' (ADR) refers to methods of resolving disputes:
o: Only through the Supreme Court of India
Outside the traditional court litigation system, through mechanisms such as arbitration, mediation, conciliation, and negotiation
Only through police intervention
Only applicable to criminal cases
questions.src: Settled ADR concept — a collective term for dispute resolution mechanisms outside conventional court litigation, including arbitration, mediation, conciliation, and negotiation

questions.q: Section 89 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 empowers courts to:
o: Dismiss all civil suits without hearing
Refer disputes, where elements of settlement exist, to ADR mechanisms such as arbitration, conciliation, mediation, or Lok Adalat, with the parties' observations
Only refer matrimonial disputes to ADR
Abolish the civil court system entirely
questions.src: CPC 1908, Section 89 — empowers courts to formulate settlement terms and refer suitable disputes to ADR mechanisms, a key statutory bridge between litigation and ADR

questions.q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes 'Arbitration' from 'Mediation' as ADR mechanisms?
o: Both result in a legally binding decision imposed by a neutral third party

Arbitration results in a binding decision (award) made by the arbitrator(s); mediation involves a neutral mediator facilitating the parties toward their own mutually agreed settlement, without imposing a decision
There is no difference between the two
Mediation is always more expensive than arbitration
questions.src: Settled ADR distinction — arbitration is adjudicatory (arbitrator decides, binding award); mediation is facilitative (mediator assists, parties decide, no imposed outcome)

questions.q: In Afcons Infrastructure Ltd. v. Cherian Varkey Construction Co. (2010), the Supreme Court provided significant guidance on:
o: The abolition of ADR mechanisms in India
The scope and application of Section 89 CPC, clarifying the categories of cases suitable for reference to arbitration, conciliation, judicial settlement, and mediation
Only criminal procedure
The Right to Information Act
questions.src: Afcons Infrastructure v. Cherian Varkey Construction (2010) — leading Supreme Court case clarifying the practical operation of Section 89 CPC and categorising disputes suitable for different ADR mechanisms

questions.q: Under Section 7 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, a valid 'arbitration agreement' must generally be:
o: Only an oral agreement, with written form being invalid

In writing (which includes a document signed by parties, an exchange of letters/electronic communications, or exchange of statements of claim/defence where existence is alleged and not denied), expressing the parties' intent to refer disputes to arbitration
Registered with the Supreme Court of India
Valid only if made in the English language
questions.src: Arbitration and Conciliation Act 1996, Section 7 — arbitration agreement must be in writing, with the section specifying recognised forms of written agreement including electronic communications

questions.q: The 'Doctrine of Kompetenz-Kompetenz', recognised under Section 16 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, refers to the principle that:
o: Only a civil court can decide whether a valid arbitration agreement exists
An arbitral tribunal has the competence/power to rule on its own jurisdiction, including objections regarding the existence or validity of the arbitration agreement, in the first instance
Arbitration agreements can never be challenged
The government has sole authority to appoint arbitrators
questions.src: Arbitration and Conciliation Act 1996, Section 16 — codifies the Kompetenz-Kompetenz doctrine, empowering the arbitral tribunal to rule on its own jurisdiction, including the existence/validity of the arbitration agreement

questions.q: Under Section 9 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, a party may apply to a court for interim measures of protection:
o: Only after the arbitral award has been passed, never before

Before, during arbitral proceedings, or at any time after the making of the arbitral award but before its enforcement, to preserve the subject matter of the dispute or otherwise protect the party's interests
Only if both parties jointly agree to seek court intervention
Never, since courts have no role once an arbitration agreement exists
questions.src: Arbitration and Conciliation Act 1996, Section 9 — allows parties to seek interim relief from court before, during, or after arbitral proceedings (before enforcement of the award), ensuring the arbitration is not rendered ineffective

questions.q: Under Section 11 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 (as amended), if parties fail to agree on the appointment of an arbitrator, the appointment may be made, upon application, by:
o: The President of India personally
The Supreme Court or the High Court (or an institution designated by them), depending on whether it is an international or domestic commercial arbitration
The local police station
Only by mutual re-negotiation with no institutional recourse
questions.src: Arbitration and Conciliation Act 1996, Section 11 (as amended by the 2015 and 2019 Amendments) — provides for court/designated-institution appointment of arbitrators where parties fail to agree, with Supreme Court handling international commercial arbitration appointments and High Courts handling domestic matters

questions.q: Under Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, an arbitral award may be set aside by a court only on specified limited grounds, which generally do NOT include:
o: The arbitration agreement being invalid
A party being unable to present its case
The award being in conflict with the public policy of India
Mere disagreement by the court with the arbitrator's assessment of evidence or interpretation of the contract (courts do not sit in appeal over the merits)
questions.src: Arbitration and Conciliation Act 1996, Section 34 — sets out a closed, limited list of grounds for setting aside an award (agreement invalidity, due process failure, public policy conflict, etc.); courts generally cannot review the merits of the arbitrator's decision as an appellate body

questions.q: Under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, a domestic arbitral award that has not been successfully challenged within the prescribed limitation period is generally:
o: Automatically void
Enforceable in the same manner as if it were a decree of a civil court
Only enforceable if the President of India approves it individually
Enforceable only against government parties
questions.src: Arbitration and Conciliation Act 1996, Section 36 — an arbitral award, once the time for challenge under Section 34 has expired (or the challenge is dismissed), is enforceable as a decree of the court

questions.q: Under Section 29B of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, parties may agree to a 'Fast Track Procedure' for arbitration, under which the arbitral tribunal is generally required to make an award within:
o: 6 months from the date the tribunal enters reference
12 months, with no exceptions
5 years
There is no time limit under the Fast Track Procedure
questions.src: Arbitration and Conciliation Act 1996, Section 29B — the Fast Track Procedure requires the award to be made within 6 months from the date the arbitral tribunal enters upon the reference, promoting speedy resolution

questions.q: 'International Commercial Arbitration' under Section 2(1)(f) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 generally refers to arbitration relating to disputes arising out of a legal relationship considered commercial, where at least one party is:
o: An individual/company/association habitually resident or incorporated or having its central management/control in a country other than India
Always the Government of India
Only a citizen of the United States
Never applicable to Indian parties under any circumstances
questions.src: Arbitration and Conciliation Act 1996, Section 2(1)(f) — defines international commercial arbitration by reference to at least one party being a foreign individual/company/association/government, in a commercial dispute

questions.q: Under Section 5 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, in matters governed by Part I of the Act, judicial authority intervention is generally:
o: Unlimited, allowing courts to intervene in arbitral proceedings at any stage for any reason
Restricted -- no judicial authority shall intervene except where so provided in Part I of the Act, reflecting the principle of minimal court interference in the arbitral process
Mandatory at every single procedural step of the arbitration
Applicable only to arbitrations seated outside India
questions.src: Arbitration and Conciliation Act 1996, Section 5 -- a non-obstante provision embodying the principle of minimal judicial intervention, restricting court interference to instances expressly provided for in Part I

questions.q: Under Part III of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, 'Conciliation' generally involves:
o: A binding decision imposed by the conciliator on the parties
A conciliator assisting the parties to reach an amicable settlement of their dispute, without the power to impose a binding decision, distinct from an arbitrator's adjudicatory role
Compulsory imprisonment of the losing party
The complete abolition of the underlying dispute with no settlement required
questions.src: Arbitration and Conciliation Act 1996, Part III (Sections 61-81) — conciliation involves a conciliator facilitating settlement, without adjudicatory power to impose a decision, similar in spirit to mediation

questions.q: In Haresh Dayaram Thakur v. State of Maharashtra (2000), the Supreme Court emphasised that conciliation proceedings are fundamentally characterised by:
o: Compulsory participation with no right to withdraw
Their voluntary nature — being based on mutual consent of the parties, with the conciliator's role being to guide the parties toward an amicable solution rather than impose one
Binding decisions similar to a court judgment
Exclusive jurisdiction of criminal courts
questions.src: Haresh Dayaram Thakur v. State of Maharashtra (2000) — Supreme Court underscored the voluntary, consent-based nature of conciliation proceedings

questions.q: The Mediation Act, 2023 was enacted with the primary objective of:
o: Abolishing all forms of ADR in India

Providing a comprehensive, dedicated statutory framework for mediation in India — covering pre-litigation mediation, online mediation, community mediation, and enforceability of mediated settlement agreements — reducing reliance on scattered mediation provisions across multiple statutes
Making litigation the only permissible dispute resolution method
Applying exclusively to criminal cases
questions.src: Mediation Act 2023 (India Code bare Act, confirmed sections in force per official notification) — consolidates mediation law into a dedicated statute, addressing pre-litigation mediation, online mediation, community mediation, and a Mediation Council of India

questions.q: Under the Mediation Act, 2023, once parties reach a mediated settlement agreement (duly signed and authenticated), the agreement is generally:
o: Merely a non-binding suggestion with no legal effect
Final and binding on the parties, and enforceable in the same manner as a judgment or decree passed by a court under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908
Automatically void after 24 hours
Enforceable only if the amount involved is below ₹10,000
questions.src: Mediation Act 2023 — a mediated settlement agreement, once signed and authenticated, is final and binding, enforceable as a court decree under the CPC 1908

questions.q: Under the Mediation Act, 2023, the body established for matters including registration, training, and continuing education of mediators is the:
o: Supreme Court Mediation Bench
Mediation Council of India
National Human Rights Commission
Bar Council of India
questions.src: Mediation Act 2023, Chapter VIII (Sections 31-38, confirmed in force per official commencement notification) — establishes the Mediation Council of India for mediator registration, training, and regulation

questions.q: Under the Mediation Act, 2023, certain categories of disputes are explicitly excluded from being resolved through mediation under the Act, including matters relating to:
o: All civil disputes without exception
Criminal prosecution/proceedings, and certain other specified categories such as matters affecting third-party rights or specified regulatory matters, as listed in the Act's schedule
Only disputes below ₹1,000
Only disputes between government departments
questions.src: Mediation Act 2023, First Schedule — lists categories of disputes not fit for mediation, including matters involving criminal prosecution/offences and other specified exclusions

questions.q: A 'Lok Adalat' organised under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 primarily functions to:
o: Impose criminal punishment on offenders

Facilitate compromise/settlement of disputes (both pending in court and at pre-litigation stage) amicably, with the award of a Lok Adalat having the status of a decree of a civil court and being final, with no appeal
Replace the Supreme Court entirely
Only handle disputes involving government land
questions.src: Legal Services Authorities Act 1987 — Lok Adalats facilitate amicable settlement; a Lok Adalat award is deemed a decree of a civil court, final, and not appealable (except in specific circumstances)

questions.q: A 'Permanent Lok Adalat', established under Section 22B of the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, is specifically empowered to:
o: Handle only criminal murder cases

Exercise jurisdiction in respect of disputes relating to 'Public Utility Services' (e.g., transport, postal, telegraph, electricity), and may decide the matter on merits if conciliation fails, subject to specified pecuniary limits
Replace all High Courts in India
Handle only disputes between two foreign nationals
questions.src: Legal Services Authorities Act 1987, Section 22B — Permanent Lok Adalats have special jurisdiction over Public Utility Service disputes and, distinctively, may decide on merits if conciliation fails

questions.q: 'Negotiation' as an ADR method is generally characterised by:
o: The mandatory presence of a neutral third party who decides the outcome
Direct discussion and bargaining between the disputing parties themselves (or their representatives), without a neutral third-party decision-maker, to reach a mutually acceptable resolution
A formal, court-supervised procedure with strict rules of evidence
Being legally binding automatically, without any agreement needed
questions.src: Settled ADR concept — negotiation is the most informal and direct ADR method, involving the parties themselves (or representatives) without a neutral decision-maker

questions.q: Under Section 10 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, parties are free to determine the number of arbitrators, provided that such number shall not be:
o: An even number
An odd number
More than one
Less than three
questions.src: Arbitration and Conciliation Act 1996, Section 10 — parties may determine the number of arbitrators, provided it is not an even number (to avoid deadlock); if not determined, the tribunal consists of a sole arbitrator

questions.q: Under Section 12 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, a person approached for possible appointment as an arbitrator must disclose in writing any circumstances likely to give rise to justifiable doubts as to their:
o: Nationality alone, with no other consideration
Independence or impartiality (including, per the Fifth and Seventh Schedules introduced by the 2015 Amendment, specified relationships/interests that may disqualify a person)
Physical fitness alone
Religious beliefs
questions.src: Arbitration and Conciliation Act 1996, Section 12 (as amended by the 2015 Amendment, introducing the Fifth and Seventh Schedules) — mandatory disclosure of circumstances affecting independence/impartiality, with certain relationships rendering a person ineligible to act as arbitrator

questions.q: The principle of 'Party Autonomy' in arbitration refers to the recognition that:
o: Courts have complete control over every aspect of the arbitration process

The parties to an arbitration agreement have significant freedom to determine key procedural aspects of their arbitration — such as the seat, the applicable procedural rules, the number of arbitrators, and the language — subject to mandatory provisions of law
Only the arbitrator has any say in how proceedings are conducted
Party autonomy has no recognition in Indian arbitration law
questions.src: Settled arbitration law principle, foundational to the 1996 Act's scheme — party autonomy allows parties to shape procedural aspects of their arbitration, subject to certain mandatory statutory provisions
